items.definition: to make pain, stress, or a problem less severe

examples.source: A short walk after lunch can alleviate the stiffness that builds up after hours at a desk.
examples.translation: Ein kurzer Spaziergang nach dem Mittagessen kann die Steifheit lindern, die sich nach Stunden am Schreibtisch aufbaut.

examples.source: The cream did not cure the condition, but it alleviated the irritation.
examples.translation: Die Creme heilte den Zustand nicht, aber sie linderte die Reizung.

examples.source: Many people find that naming their anxiety aloud can alleviate some of its intensity.
examples.translation: Viele Menschen erleben, dass das laute Benennen ihrer Angst einen Teil ihrer Intensität lindern kann.

items.definition: containing a high level of beneficial nutrients relative to calories

examples.source: Her coach encouraged her to build meals around nutrient-dense foods rather than around restrictions alone.
examples.translation: Ihr Coach riet ihr, Mahlzeiten eher um nährstoffreiche Lebensmittel als nur um Verbote herum aufzubauen.

examples.source: Soup can be surprisingly nutrient-dense if it includes beans, vegetables and a good source of protein.
examples.translation: Suppe kann überraschend nährstoffreich sein, wenn sie Bohnen, Gemüse und eine gute Eiweißquelle enthält.

examples.source: When energy is low, reaching for something convenient is understandable, but nutrient-dense choices usually help more in the long run.
examples.translation: Wenn die Energie niedrig ist, greift man verständlicherweise zu etwas Bequemem, aber nährstoffreiche Entscheidungen helfen langfristig meist mehr.

examples.source: Mild dehydration often shows up first as fatigue or difficulty concentrating.

examples.source: The nurse explained how quickly dehydration becomes more serious in very hot weather.

items.definition: to continue doing something or to follow a plan consistently

examples.source: The hardest part of any health plan is often not starting but sticking to it.

examples.source: He found it easier to stick to a routine once he linked it to his morning coffee.

examples.source: People are more likely to stick to exercise when it fits their real life rather than an idealised schedule.

pages.text: After months of feeling slightly off, Lena decided to stop treating her health as something that would somehow improve on its own. Her symptoms were not dramatic, but a persistent tiredness had started to colour everything: work, family evenings and even weekends. The doctor was reassuring. Nothing urgent appeared in the tests, yet the consultation made one thing clear: her daily routine was far more sedentary than she had admitted to herself, and her meals were quick but rarely nutrient-dense.

Rather than chasing a miracle solution, Lena began with modest changes. She tried to stick to a more regular bedtime, walked after lunch and kept a bottle of water close by because mild dehydration had become normal without her noticing it. She also paid attention to the habits that seemed to ward off stress rather than intensify it. On difficult days she used stretching and slow breathing to alleviate tension and to regulate her energy more gently.

A few weeks later she came down with a minor cold, which felt discouraging at first. But even that interruption taught her something useful. Recovery did not mean doing everything perfectly; it meant learning how to make a recovery without giving up on the larger routine. By the end of the season, the difference was not dramatic enough for anyone else to applaud, yet it was real enough for Lena to feel she had reclaimed some authority over her own body.
